name: Third Battle of Panipat
info: On 14 January 1761 the Durrani Empire and its Indian allies defeated the Maratha army at Panipat, 97 kilometres north of Delhi; tens of thousands of Marathas died in the fighting and after it.

facts.date: 14 January 1761, after skirmishing and a siege of about two months
facts.place: In and around the city of Panipat, about 97 kilometres (60 mi) north of Delhi, in present-day India
facts.sides: The Maratha Empire under Sadashivrao Bhau, with an army put at between 45,000 and 60,000 and roughly 200,000 non-combatants; the Durrani Empire under Ahmad Shah Durrani (Abdali), with Najib-ud-Daula, the Rohillas and Shuja-ud-Daula of Oudh. Over 125,000 troops are given for the whole battle.
facts.outcome: The Afghan army won after several Maratha flanks were destroyed. Between 60,000 and 70,000 troops are believed to have been killed in the fighting, and about 40,000 Maratha prisoners were killed the next day according to an eyewitness chronicle.

t: The battle brought the Maratha Empire, whose rule had reached north of the Indus in 1758, into direct conflict with the Durrani Empire, which the Marathas' hold on Punjab and Delhi had threatened.
The Marathas were besieged for about two months in their lines, and Sadashivrao Bhau led them out on 13 January because supplies had run short.
The killing did not end with the fighting: the best eyewitness chronicle reports about 40,000 prisoners killed the day after, and about 22,000 women and children were taken as slaves.
dyk: The battle perhaps had the largest number of fatalities in a single day reported in a classic formation battle between two armies, and the Marathas brought roughly 200,000 non-combatants, among them pilgrims, with their army.
ev: The Marathas take Lahore with Adina Beg Khan and drive out Timur Shah Durrani, extending their rule north of the Indus
Ahmad Shah Durrani raises an army and wins over Najib-ud-Daula, the Rohillas and Shuja-ud-Daula
The Maratha army under Sadashivrao Bhau starts north from Patdur
The Afghans cross the Yamuna at Baghpat and skirmish at Samalkha, which leaves the Marathas partly encircled
The Marathas leave their camp before dawn on 13 January and face the Afghan lines at about eight in the morning
The main battle is fought on 14 January; Vishwasrao is killed and the Maratha lines break
Prisoners are killed the day after the battle and women and children are driven off as slaves
Ahmad Shah leaves for Afghanistan, with the Sikhs harassing his march through Punjab

sections.background:
In 1757 Ahmad Shah Durrani made his son Timur Shah governor of Punjab. Jahan Khan, who ruled for the young governor, was harsh, and Adina Beg Khan, the governor of Jalandhar Doab, turned to the Marathas, who had taken Delhi after the Battle of Delhi (1757). With his help the Marathas and Sikhs drove the Afghans from Lahore, and in 1758 Adina Beg was made subahdar of the Punjab in return for a yearly tribute of seventy five lakh of rupees.

This was the high-water mark of Maratha expansion, with their rule running from north of the Indus to northern Kerala, and the Peshwa spoke of placing his son Vishwasrao on the Mughal throne. Shah Waliullah and other Muslim clergy were alarmed and appealed to Ahmad Shah Abdali. In 1759 he raised an army whose core was Qizilbash, with Pashtun tribes, Kurds and Uzbeks, and joined the Rohillas, other Muslims of northern India and Shuja-ud-Daula, the Nawab of Awadh, who by late July 1760 chose what was seen as the army of Islam.

The Maratha command went to Sadashivrao Bhau after Raghunathrao asked for more troops than Bhau, his cousin, would give and declined to go north. Bhau gathered between 45,000 and 60,000 troops, with roughly 200,000 non-combatants, some of them pilgrims bound for Hindu holy sites.
sections.forces:
The battle set the artillery, musketry and cavalry of the Marathas against the heavy cavalry, jezail musketry and mounted zamburak artillery of the Afghans and Rohillas under Ahmad Shah Durrani and Najib-ud-Daula. Over 125,000 troops were involved. The Marathas had almost 150 French-made guns, with a range of over a kilometre, and Bhau planned to break the Afghans with cannon fire and to hold his cavalry back. Durrani had numerical and qualitative superiority, and the Maratha artillery was static and lacked mobility.

Before the battle the Jat ruler Suraj Mal advised leaving the families and baggage behind and fighting with light cavalry. Bhau found this dishonourable, and the Jats later withdrew their support. The Marathas, besieged for two months, were cut off by Afghan forces on every side. Bhau led out his army on 13 January, with Ibrahim Khan Gardi's musketeers on the left, Holkar and Sindhia on the right and himself with the Peshwa's son in the centre. The line was about 12 km across, with the civilians behind it.

The Afghan line lay a few metres south of today's Sanauli Road. Najib held the left, Shuja-ud-Daula, with 3,000 soldiers and 50 to 60 cannon, and the vizier Shah Wali, with 19,000 mailed horsemen, held the left centre, and 15,000 Rohillas under Hafiz Rahmat the right centre. Ahmad Shah stood in the rear of the line and had 60 smooth-bore cannon.
sections.course:
Before dawn on 14 January the Marathas broke their fast on sugared water and moved their guns into place about 2 km from the Afghans. Ibrahim Khan's infantry led the attack, the first Afghan charge by Najib's Rohillas was broken, and for three hours the 8,000 Gardi musketeers killed about 12,000 Rohillas. Bhau then led a charge at the Afghan left centre under Shah Wali, which nearly broke the line, but the Marathas' half-starved horses were exhausted. Shuja-ud-Daula held his place, and Ahmad Shah sent musketeers to shoot deserters back into the field.

By noon it looked as though Bhau would win. Ahmad Shah called up 15,000 reserve troops and 2,000 swivel-mounted camel guns, which fired over the heads of his own infantry at the Maratha cavalry. About 7,000 Maratha cavalry and infantry were killed before hand-to-hand fighting began at about 14:00, and by 16:00 the tired infantry gave way to fresh Afghan reserves.

Bhau came down from his elephant to lead the fight, and Vishwasrao had already been killed by a shot to the head. Afghan prisoners taken at Kunjpura are said to have risen within the Maratha camp, and Vitthal Vinchurkar and Damaji Gaikwad broke position, leaving the Gardis to be encircled. Some Maratha artillery fought until sunset, and many troops escaped that night.
sections.aftermath:
Between 60,000 and 70,000 troops are believed to have been killed in the fighting; the extent of the losses on both sides is heavily disputed, and the numbers of injured and prisoners vary considerably. After the defeat the Afghans, Mughals, Rohillas and Awadh troops fell on the fleeing Marathas and killed soldiers and civilians. Afghan officers who had lost kin were allowed to carry out massacres the next day, in Panipat and around it, and heaped mounds of severed heads outside their camps.

According to the bakhar of Kashi Raja, the diwan of Shuja-ud-Daula, about 40,000 Maratha prisoners were killed the day after the battle. Hamilton, a reporter of the Bombay Gazette, also gives 40,000 executed. Qutb Shah's son killed 4,000 fugitives near Sonepat and Abdus Samad Khan's son 5,000 near Bahadurgad, and some 22,000 women and children were driven off as slaves. Sikhs under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia are said to have saved 2,000 of the prisoners. The Siyar-ut-Mutakhirin describes prisoners paraded, given parched grain and water, and beheaded.

Jankoji Scindia was taken and executed at Najib's instigation, and Ibrahim Khan Gardi was tortured and executed. Bhau's wife Parvatibai escaped to Pune, and some 15,000 soldiers reached Gwalior. Ahmad Shah named Najib-ud-Daula regent to the Mughal emperor and left for Afghanistan in March 1761.
sections.sources:
The single best eyewitness chronicle is the bakhar by Kashi Raja, the diwan of Shuja-ud-Daula, who was an ally of the Afghans. The British historian Grant Duff's History of the Marathas includes an interview with a survivor of the massacres and generally corroborates the figure of 40,000, and the Siyar-ut-Mutakhirin also describes them. Shejwalkar's monograph Panipat 1761 is often regarded as the best secondary source, and his own total is not less than 100,000 Marathas, soldiers and non-combatants, killed during and after the battle.

The figures are where the accounts part. The losses on both sides are heavily disputed and the numbers of injured and prisoners vary considerably. The 60,000 to 70,000 killed in the fighting is what historians are said to believe, not a count. The Bombay Gazette's Hamilton puts about half a million Marathi people in Panipat town, while the figure given for the Maratha non-combatants on the march is roughly 200,000.

Historians also differ on why the Marathas lost. Accounts of the defeat list Afghan numbers and mobility, the quarrels among Maratha chiefs, the distance of about 1,000 km from Pune and Bhau's lack of knowledge of northern India. Some hold that guerrilla warfare, as Holkar and Suraj Mal advised, could not have been carried out with the camp followers, and that if Holkar had stayed the defeat would have been delayed but not averted.
sections.legacy:
The Marathas never fully recovered from Panipat but remained the largest empire in the Indian subcontinent and retook Delhi ten years later. The result was a temporary halt to their advance in the north and about ten years of destabilisation. Madhavrao is credited with reviving their power, and in 1771 Mahadji Shinde led an army into the north to restore Maratha supremacy. After Madhavrao's early death, at 28, the chiefs fell into infighting, and the East India Company annexed their lands in 1819.

For the Punjab, the Durrani victory ended Maratha plans to take it and left the Durranis and the Sikhs as the two main powers. The Sikhs harassed Ahmad Shah's march home, and the Jats under Suraj Mal, who stayed out of the battle, are said to have helped the Marathas who escaped. The Rohillas were rewarded with grants, and the Mughal empire, still nominal, officially ended in 1857.

Ahmad Shah praised the Marathas' valour in a letter to Madho Singh of Jaipur, and the battle is also remembered as a scene of valour on both sides. It has been the subject of a poem by Kipling, a Bengali poem by Kaykobad, a play by Munier Choudhury, a Marathi novel by Vishwas Patil and a 2019 film that has several major historical inaccuracies.

summary: The Third Battle of Panipat, fought on 14 January 1761, pitted the Maratha Empire against the Durrani Empire and its Indian allies. The Afghan side won. An eyewitness chronicle reports about 40,000 Maratha prisoners killed the next day, and some 22,000 women and children were driven off as slaves.
notes: The article gives 'over 125,000 troops' for the battle as a whole, with no separate Afghan total; Maratha 45,000 to 60,000 is for the army only.
Hamilton's half a million Marathi people in Panipat conflicts with the roughly 200,000 non-combatants; both are kept, attributed.
The article's 'Shah Shuja's forces played a decisive role in intelligence' is unclear (Shuja-ud-Daula?) and was left out.
Abdali's letter praising Maratha valour contains 'wretched Deccanis'; not quoted. The Kunjpura massacre, Samalkha losses and the Meerut deaths were left out for space.
Dates: the Afghan crossing of the Yamuna is 23 to 25 October 1760; the siege 'two months' is the article's.
Not found in the article: the Afghan army's total size, a Maratha loss figure for the day other than 7,000 in the cavalry exchange, the Afghan losses.
